10c907b47c68bd: Objects you use or see every day that you probably never thought had a date and place of invention.
0373ccffd0ef99:
The wheel hasn't always existed

It's easy to forget that the wheel had to be invented — it isn't a "natural" object like a rock or a stick. The oldest archaeological evidence of wheels used for transport comes from Mesopotamia, around 3500 BC, first as potter's wheels (for shaping pottery) and shortly after adapted to transport carts.

🛞 A fun fact: the potter's wheel is probably older than the transport wheel — meaning it was first used to shape pottery by spinning clay, and only later did someone have the idea of turning it on its side to move things.

The plow: multiplying the food supply

The ox-drawn plow made it possible to work much more land with the same human effort, further increasing the agricultural surplus you saw in class 2 — a self-reinforcing loop: more food, more people free to specialize, more inventions.

Other lesser-known inventions

  • The first planned irrigation system: canals to carry river water to fields far from the bank.
  • Beer: one of the oldest documented fermented drinks — in fact, part of workers' wages was paid in rations of beer.
  • The first known map: a tablet depicting the city of Nippur with remarkable geographic accuracy.
💡 None of these inventions arose in isolation — the wheel, the plow and irrigation reinforce each other, each one making the others more efficient.
